'''''Ranunculus sceleratus''''' known by the common names '''celery-leaved buttercup''',<ref name=NHM>{{cite web |url=http://www.nhm.ac.uk/our-science/data/uk-species/species/ranunculus_sceleratus.html |title=''Ranunculus sceleratus'', Celery-leaved buttercup |publisher=Natural History Museum |location=London |access-date=27 May 2016 }}</ref> '''celery-leaf buttercup''',<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Lee |editor1-first=Sangtae |editor2-last=Chang |editor2-first=Kae Sun |title=English Names for Korean Native Plants |year=2015 |publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]] |location=Pocheon |isbn=978-89-97450-98-5 |page=602 |url=http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf |access-date=15 March 2019 |via=[[Korea Forest Service]]}}</ref> and '''cursed buttercup'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RASC3|taxon=Ranunculus sceleratus|accessdate=18 Oct 2015}}</ref> is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the buttercup family [[Ranunculaceae]]. It has a circumpolar distribution in the northern hemisphere, native to temperate and boreal [[North America]] and [[Eurasia]], where it grows in wet and moist habitats, including ponds and streambanks.

==Description==
[[File:Imperial Encyclopaedia - Plant Kingdom - pic099 - 石龍芮圖.png|thumb|''Ranunculus sceleratus'' (石龍芮) diagram in ''[[Gujin Tushu Jicheng]]'' encyclopedia by [[Chen Menglei]]]]
''Ranunculus sceleratus'' is an annual herb growing up to half a meter tall. The leaves are more or less [[glossary of botanical terms#glabrous|glabrous]] (hairless) and have small blades each deeply lobed or divided into three leaflets. They are borne on long [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]]. The flowers are 5-10mm across with five or fewer yellow petals a few millimeters long and reflexed [[sepal]]s. The fruit is an [[achene]] borne in a cluster of several.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2010|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Third|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location = Cambridge, U.K.| isbn=978-0-521-70772-5}}</ref>{{rp|110,114}}

While buttercups are toxic due to the presence of the substance [[protoanemonin]], this applies in particular for the cursed buttercup: it is the most toxic buttercup and contains 2.5% protoanemonin. When the leaves are wrinkled, damaged or crushed, they bring out unsightly sores and blisters on human skin. All parts of the plant are considered to be poisonous. Side effects after ingestion can manifest themselves as extremely irritating to the skin and mucous membranes. It may cause sensation of pain and burning perceptions, tongue inflammation, and intensification in salivation.<ref name="FH">{{Cite journal | last= Abid Aqsa, Mushtaq Ahmad, Muhammad Zafar, Sadia Zafar, Mohamed Fawzy Ramadan, Ashwaq T. Althobaiti, Shazia Sultana, Omer Kilic, Trobjon Makhkamov, Akramjon Yuldashev, Oybek Mamarakhimov, Khislat Khaydarov, Afat O. Mammadova, Komiljon Komilov |first= and Salman Majeed |date=December 2023|title= Foliar epidermal and trichome micromorphological diversity among poisonous plants and their taxonomic significance|journal=[[Folia Horticulturae]]|language=en|volume=35|issue=2|pages=243 – 274|doi= 10.2478/fhort-2023-0019 |issn=2083-5965|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Ranunculus sceleratus'' has a circumpolar distribution in the northern hemisphere<ref name=DVF>{{cite web|url=http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/ranuncula/ranun/ranuscev.jpg|first=Arne|last=Anderberg|title=''Ranunculus sceleratus'' (L.) Sw|publisher=Naturhistoriska riksmuseet, Stockholm |access-date=27 May 2016 }}</ref> There are two varieties and one subspecies<ref name=PlantList>{{cite web| title=The Plant List: ''Ranunculus sceleratus'' L |date=2013 |url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2526806 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew and Missouri Botanic Garden |access-date=27 May 2016}}</ref> with distinctive distributions: ''R. sceleratus'' ssp. ''reptabundus'' occurs in northern [[Finland]] and north-west [[Russia]].<ref name=DVF/> ''R. scleratus'' var. ''multifidus'' occurs in north western [[North America]],<ref name=DVF/> and ''R. scleratus'' var. ''longissimus'' is found from Minnesota to Alabama according to their biodiversity and plant atlases respectively.{{citation needed|date=August 2018}} It is also distributed in Australia and New Zealand.<ref name=IUCN/>
